anti_overlap: Defers to fd-crisis-action-gating on availability timing; focuses on budget/cost mechanics
decision_lens: Budget fairness — deployment actions should compete fairly with policy actions for budget slots without creating dominant strategies
focus: How do deploy/withdraw actions interact with the observation/action budget — crowding, zero-cost gaming, portfolio allocation?
name: fd-budget-interaction
persona: Resource economics analyst who models budget allocation strategies under constraints and identifies dominant strategies
review_areas: Do deployment actions consume the same action budget as policy actions?
Can a model exhaust its budget purely on deployments, starving policy actions?
Is there a separate deployment budget, and if so how does it interact with the main budget?
Could zero-cost deployments (if any) be exploited to game the scoring system?
Does the budget system need rebalancing for the expanded action space?
What's the optimal deploy-to-policy ratio, and can models converge on it trivially?

severity_examples.scenario: Deploy actions are free (don't consume budget), so rational models always deploy everywhere

severity_examples.condition: Budget creates false tradeoff that doesn't reflect strategic thinking
severity_examples.scenario: Budget is so tight that adding deploy/withdraw means models can't do both policy AND deployment

severity_examples.condition: No genuine tradeoff between action types
severity_examples.scenario: Optimal strategy is always 'deploy first, policy second' making budget allocation trivial

success_hints: Deployment actions create a genuine portfolio allocation challenge where models must balance deployment vs. policy investments
task_context: Open question from brainstorm: how do deployments interact with the existing observation/action budget?
